citations.B1: Read-then-write on `counts` is not atomic, so two threads can both read 99 and both admit
citations.B3: replace with an atomic increment (`itertools.count`, a lock around the whole check-and-update, or a check on the post-increment value)
citations.B4: There is no time window at all — a user is capped forever after 100 requests instead of per second/minute; use a fixed-window key including a timestamp bucket, or a token bucket with a refill.
citations.B5: Nothing ever removes entries, so `counts` grows without bound for every user_id ever seen — expire keys (Redis TTL) or evict on window rollover.
citations.B6: The dict itself lives per process, so N workers each grant the full limit and the effective cap is N×limit — move the counter to a shared store
citations.B7: `user_id` is unvalidated, so `None`, an empty string, or an unbounded attacker-supplied string becomes a permanent dict key — validate type and length before use, and reject absent identifiers
